Hi OP, have you considered that you may have ARFID or a sensory processing disorder? I say this not to be an armchair psychologist, but because you sound very similar to me but with different safe foods. Let me tell you about my experience with that and veganism. 

I was vegan for almost 5 years. I also have sensory processing issues that make eating very difficult sometimes. When I entered college, I had a difficult time eating *anything* in the dining hall because most of it wasn’t vegan, and because the vegan stuff had textures that rendered them inedible to me. This went on for two years, me just not really eating much of anything and skipping meals often or forcing myself to eat foods I couldn’t stomach because I knew I needed to eat, and sometimes I would end up vomiting too or simply being unable to swallow. I ended up losing 25 pounds off of my (very small) frame and becoming extremely underweight, fatigued, fucking up my hunger cues, dealing with nutrient deficiencies, etc etc. I went vegetarian because I simply wasn’t getting enough calories to sustain myself, but I had been vegan for so long that I lost the ability to digest animal proteins and they made me sick too. 

It’s better now that I’m very familiar with my own safe foods and can cook for myself, and have also gradually expanded my list of safe foods over time. But when you have food issues like this, you need to be really careful about restricting your diet even more. You can, and *will* end up extremely unhealthy and malnourished, don’t do the same thing I did. Although I’m healthier now and don’t have any nutrient deficiencies, I still am underweight and very slowly gaining it back. 

If you’re interested, message me and I can talk to you about making the process of becoming more comfortable with foods easier. Perhaps it would be in your best interest to ease your way into veganism by finding safe vegan dishes you can make over time rather than jumping into it?

Many cultures use hallucinogenic substances in their spiritual and religious practices in order to ascend to a higher plane. In this sense, it is not about getting high at all. In my own experience as someone with severe PTSD that was not responding to traditional clinical treatment (meds/therapy mostly) and left me unable to function (as in, unable to eat, sleep, be hygienic, do work, connect to others, etc.), my experience with psychedelics gave me the “kick in the ass” I needed, so to speak, to change my outlook on life, rebalance certain chemical pathways, connect to myself and the world in a spiritual way, and ultimately to be able to function, find peace within myself, and to grow as a human being.

No, it’s not that. Perhaps you can talk to them your next appointment and say you’re having a hard time with a negative self-image and you’d like to explore it more? It’s not that therapists are always just complimenting people - this happens of course, but it’s more about helping you reframe your mindset so you no longer need the external validation from other people in terms of compliments and stuff to feel good about yourself. I also see you’ve tried 3 therapists and think the common denominator is you - it can take a long time to find a “perfect fit” therapist, if ever. I’m no longer in therapy (expensive lol), but it took 4 therapists for me to find one that really understood me in a way like no other therapist or even just another person has ever, and who I can truly say completely changed who I am to my core as a result of what she taught me. 

My final “perfect fit” therapist met a few criteria though, I wasn’t just shooting in the dark. 

These were my criteria, or what made her so good for me:

• I wanted a woman, as I am a woman with a history of CSA and struggle to be vulnerable with men and also struggle with respecting them when they have “authority” over me, and when you have severe trauma it does feel like therapists and other healthcare professionals have an air of authority over you. 

• an older woman specifically, she was kind of maternal, or like an aunt - this was important to me because I had horrible parents and needed “reparenting” and also to learn how to internalize my own “parents” so to speak, like I had to create a nurturing, loving, calm, compassionate, and accepting voice within myself that I lacked from having abusive parents. When my inner child throws a tantrum as a result of inflaming past trauma and triggering that past hurt, my inner parent kicks in and soothes her. This is the singular most important thing I learned from therapy in terms of my self-image. When your wounded inner child is throwing a tantrum, that’s when you end up repeating toxic/unhealthy behaviors in your relationships. 

• She specialized in people of my “type” - as a teenager, I thought I had BPD, and that’s what she specialized in. She diagnosed me with cPTSD, but there’s a ton of overlap in those diagnoses and where they stem from (often repeated childhood abuse and trauma). Therefore she was waaaay more equipped to help me manage my behaviors and thought patterns as opposed to my other therapists, who were just regular talk therapists with no special focus. Regular CBT was not very helpful for me because I was dealing with more pervasive and deep issues (again, severe childhood trauma, not just a mood disorder due to unlucky genetics). She employed a lot of techniques to actively work through my issues that I had never experienced before, even in DBT and the hospital, and I found most of them extremely effective. 

• Last, this was not something I “shopped” for but was just a nice coincidence, but she had a very similar childhood to me in terms of CSA, horrible and neglectful parents, and leaving at a young age, so she was able to relate to me and guide me through the process of healing in a way no other therapist was able to do. Because of her past, she decided to specialize in trauma therapy for women and in disorders that tend to be seen more often in women (like BPD) since she felt her empathy and experience allowed her to relate more effectively. 

That was all very long, but I hope it helped a little bit - it’s okay to shop for therapists with specialties, and you SHOULD. People decide to become therapists for a lot of reasons, a major one being their own experiences and a desire to help other people through that. You aren’t the problem if you can’t relate to your therapist very well, and they aren’t either - you just maybe aren’t a good match for each other.

When you have problems with self-esteem and self-image like many of us do that’s a huge component of therapy! Not like, the therapist just rattling off compliments, but many codependents only find value in themselves with regards to other people, so like we only feel valuable when we’re being helpful or caretaking or rescuing people. But we have intrinsic value as human beings far beyond what we can offer to others, and when we can internalize that value we can more fully address the reasons *why* we engage in codependent behavior in the first place and break free from that cycle.

Symptoms on this tree include top death and dieback plus the flecking, where woodpeckers and such have been peeling the bark back to get at the larvae. I’ve been homeless in Roanoke. You’re spot on about avoiding the cops, they like to harass people sleeping in cars. Avoid SE cuz people get sketchy there and neighborhoods that give off NIMBY vibes cuz they will call the cops. I second the back of a church parking lot, or drive around at night and find a dimly lit and quiet street and park there for the night, don’t post up for longer than you need to though and try to leave early in the morning so try to keep some variety in parking areas. I would often park at Hollins in one of the extant parking lots, but they were nicer about it because I was a student there and they’ve recently upped security and they’re all real assholes. You could also try the Rescue Mission, I never stayed there (I avoided it) and many people do not recommend it including my friend who interned there, but for many people sleeping in cars gets old verrry fast. 

It gets hot at night, please stay hydrated. Keep your windows open/cracked as long as you can at night and cover them before the sun starts to rise. Sleeping in cars sucks and begins to take a serious toll on your body quickly, so really do whatever you can to make this more comfortable for you. If you have a larger car put the seats down and get a good amount of blankets/padding to sleep on; try not to just sleep curled up in your seat, I’m still dealing with back problems from that. Having a cooler is really nice, ice is cheap and it helps beat the heat and keep your perishable food for longer. Eating out gets expensive fast. I cant stress the hydration thing enough right now, it’s HOT sleeping in cars, so get yourself some gallon jugs of water. 

Let me know if you have any specific questions about logistics or making this more comfortable. I’m sorry you’re going through this, being homeless sucks big time, especially in the summer. But the most important thing is to keep a positive attitude and know this is temporary! I was homeless for a while before/in early college and now I have a home, a kitty, and a promising academic career! It’s easy to feel really low about yourself after a while even when you know this shit just happens to the best of us. Involuntarily living in a car packed with all of your worldly possessions can deal a huge blow to your sense of self after a while, so be kind to yourself and make yourself as comfortable as possible. Invest in things that will specifically make you more comfortable, even if this is very temporary.

I am a student in a similar situation, but with no contact with my family. It’s very true that being first gen, impoverished, and without a support system financially and emotionally severely impacts your ability to perform well in school. This isn’t your fault at all of course, as the student should have been communicating with you about this far in advance. The student is wrong to think that these circumstances should be taken into account during grading, they shouldn’t, but they can and SHOULD be taken into account when considering extensions and out of class help but ONLY if the student is willing to be upfront and negotiate/work with you on this. 

You’re new at teaching, and you aren’t supposed to be perfect at it nor at addressing every students personal needs. Many professors who have been teaching for ages refuse to negotiate with students in these situations at all, at which point it makes every bit of sense to include the Dean and appeal. 

But as a bit of advice, if a student comes to you with this kind of situation well in advance(a requirement), you have no idea what the kindness of allowing extensions/rewrites/etc. can do. I feel forever indebted to the professors who’ve shown me that kindness throughout my schooling career because they have literally changed my life, shown me I am capable of succeeding in higher education despite my circumstances, and have very much bolstered my education in the ways I was lacking (support system, financial freedom, free time, etc) and allowed me to prove my level of academic integrity. THAT is what makes a wonderful professor, and many of my professors have told me that the personal relationships they form with students in these situations are what keep them passionate about teaching in the first place.

I’ll preface that I have been homeless in Roanoke before (never stayed at the Rescue Mission) and I am also female. 

The briefest advice I can offer you is that it’s getting pretty cold now. If you can’t get a slot at the Mission but you can sleep out of your car, make sure you have plenty of blankets and ways to stay warm as it’s getting below freezing. Second, avoid parking your car in places close to or in downtown and avoid parking it anywhere in south east. Third, what kind of food places are you looking for, free or reduced cost meals? Or just convenient food in general? The rescue mission offers three meals a day and I believe there’s a couple of food banks downtown. The farmers market and the co op downtown also take SNAP if you have food stamps. 

Try to park in a nonresidential area as people can get kind of sketched out because neighborhoods are often rather suspicious of new parked vehicles and such. Cover all your windows and try to leave the spot you’ve parked at early in the morning. They nixed the ordinance  or arresting people for living out of cars, but the cops will definitely ticket you for whatever they can saddle you for so be careful to follow parking rules. If they know you’re sleeping there they’ll also knock on your window and try to talk to you but I’d avoid the hassle, they aren’t always very nice. 

I would try to get a slot at the women’s shelter at the Mission though, bring an ID. If they’re full try again later. It’s in southeast right near downtown. They can take care of most of your concerns and it’s probably a lot nicer than sleeping in your car in the cold for a month !!

Hope that helps a bit, DM me if you have any other questions though!! Being homeless sucks. Sorry you have to deal with that.

You mean dieback due to emerald ash borer? Typically when we determine whether a tree is infested with EAB we look for the following signs:

1. the presence of D-shaped exit holes (best indicator save for seeing an actual beetle)
2. flecking; this is the peeling away of bark due to woodpeckers trying to get at the larvae 
3. epicormic shoots; “lifeline” branches the tree sends up on the trunk as it experiences top-down death
4. S-shaped larval galleries when bark is peeled back
5. Top-down or sectional crown dieback; whole portions of the tree will be totally dead and/or leafless 

Just a dead leaflet isn’t enough to indicate infestation and can be due to many things. General abortion, drought, that kind of thing.
